pages.title: Before you begin
paragraphs: The craving is withdrawal wearing the mask of hunger. See it once and it loosens.
The excerpt is drawn from the English sample text currently available on this site. This is not a complete edition.

pages.title: The afternoon walk to the kitchen
paragraphs:
Start with the moment itself. It is late afternoon, the part of the day when your attention thins out, and something in you turns toward the kitchen. You are not deciding anything. Your feet are already moving. By the time you notice, the wrapper is open and the first bite is gone, and a small voice says there, that is better.

Hold on to that voice, because it is the whole trap in one sentence. It promised you that you were about to feel better. And for a few seconds, you did.

The question this book asks, patiently and completely, is a simple one: better than what.

Here is what actually happened in your body. An hour or two before that walk to the kitchen, your blood sugar had climbed and then fallen, the ordinary aftermath of the last sweet thing you ate. The fall is what you felt as the thinning of attention, the flat restless mood, the vague idea that something was wrong and food would fix it. That feeling was not hunger.

It was the withdrawal from the last hit, wearing the costume of a craving for the next one.

This is the move the trap makes over and over. It creates a small discomfort, then offers itself as the cure for that discomfort. The relief is real, which is exactly why the lie is so convincing. You are not imagining the better feeling. You are simply crediting it to the wrong thing. The sugar did not lift you above your normal baseline.

It returned you, briefly, to the baseline it had pulled you below in the first place.

Picture someone who puts a small stone in each shoe every morning, and then, every afternoon, sells themselves the beautiful relief of taking the stones out. The relief is genuine. They really do feel better with the stones gone. But they are not ahead. They are back where a person without stones stays all day, for free, without the ritual and without the ache in between.

You have been told the problem is willpower, that if you were a little stronger you would walk past the kitchen. Notice how neatly that story serves the trap. It keeps your attention on you, on your supposed weakness, and away from the mechanism doing the actual work. As long as you believe the pull is a moral failing, you will fight it with guilt, and guilt is a fuel the trap runs on beautifully.

So we are going to do something different in these pages.

We are not going to build your discipline up like a muscle for a fight. We are going to take the fight apart, because a belief that has been seen clearly cannot be un-seen, and a craving that has lost its story has nothing left to stand on.

For now, all that is asked of you is to watch. The next time your feet turn toward the kitchen, do not resist and do not obey. Just look.

pages.title: Before you begin
paragraphs: For when the feed owns your evenings and your attention feels rented. This book takes the scrolling trap apart piece by piece: where the pull comes from, what it actually delivers, and why stopping will feel like relief rather than loss.
The excerpt is drawn from the English sample text currently available on this site. This is not a complete edition.

pages.title: The reach
paragraphs:
You reached for your phone just now, or a few minutes ago, and you could not have said why. There was no message you were waiting for, no fact you needed. Your hand moved on its own, the way it has learned to, into the small bright world that is always one tap away. That reach is where we begin, because it is where the trap lives, not in the phone but in the reaching.

Let us be precise about what you were looking for. It was not information.

If it were information, you would stop when you had it. You were looking for the next thing, and then the next, and the defining feature of the next thing is that it never arrives. The scroll is designed as a horizon: something is always about to appear that is better than what is on the screen right now. You are not consuming content. You are chasing a promise that renews itself faster than you can catch it.

This is worth sitting with, because it explains the strange emptiness afterward.

When you finish a good meal you feel full. When you finish a good book you feel something completed in you. When you look up from twenty minutes of scrolling, you feel neither full nor complete. You feel slightly worse than before, and vaguely annoyed at yourself, and you could not name one thing you saw. That is not a side effect of the trap. That is the trap working exactly as intended.

The belief holding it all together is quiet and rarely said out loud: that the next screen is where the good thing is. Not this one, the next one. As long as you believe that, you cannot stop, because stopping would mean walking away one screen before the payoff. So you stay, and the payoff stays one screen ahead, and the machine that built this understood your attention better than you have ever been invited to understand it yourself.

You have probably tried to fix this with force.

App timers, a home screen swept clean, the phone left in another room. These can help for a day or two, the way holding your breath helps against a bad smell. But force treats the reaching as the enemy, and the reaching is not the enemy. It is a symptom of the belief. Change the belief and the reaching quiets on its own. Fight the reaching while the belief stands, and you have signed up for a battle with no end.

Notice, too, how the trap has taught you to describe yourself. Addicted. Weak.

Bad with phones. Every one of those words points the blame inward and leaves the design untouched. You were not weak. You were up against something engineered by large teams of clever people to be exactly this hard to put down, and no one warned you that was the game. Knowing that is not an excuse. It is the first honest map of the ground you are standing on.

Over the next chapters we will take this apart calmly.
